opus-5.5.text:
I think the relationship has changed a lot over the past few years. There used to be a fairly clear pipeline: research teams explored ideas, published papers, and some of those ideas were eventually picked up by product teams, often years later. That gap has shrunk dramatically. With large language models, the distance between a research breakthrough and something users can touch can be a matter of months, sometimes weeks.

So now it's much more of a two-way street. Research still needs room to explore things that may not pay off for a long time, and I think it's important to protect that, because many of the ideas that matter most today started out looking fairly academic. But product also feeds back into research in a way it didn't before. When millions of people use a model, you quickly learn where it fails, what people actually care about, and which capabilities matter in practice versus which just look good on a benchmark. That signal is incredibly valuable for deciding what to work on next.

The challenge is balance. If everything becomes driven by the next product launch, you risk losing the longer-horizon work that creates the next generation of capabilities. If research is too disconnected, you build things nobody can use. What works best, in my experience, is having researchers who understand the product constraints and product people who understand what the models can and can't do, and letting them work closely enough that ideas flow quickly in both directions.

r001.rationale: The response describes bringing research closer to products users can use, but it does not identify this as a goal shared by Google Brain and Andrew Dai’s current company.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the honest answer is that the line between the two has gotten a lot blurrier than it used to be, and I think that's a good thing.

A few years ago you could draw a pretty clean picture: research lives in one building, they publish papers, and maybe once in a while something gets thrown over the wall and a product team figures out what to do with it. That model is mostly dead now. The pace is such that if a research result sits around for six months, it's stale. So the loop has to be tight.

The way I think about it, there are really two directions of flow. One is research pushing capabilities into product. A model gets better at reasoning, or handles longer context, or becomes more reliable at tool use, and suddenly an entire category of product that wasn't viable last quarter becomes viable. Product people have to be close enough to the research to see that coming, not just react to it after a launch.

The other direction, which I think people underrate, is product pulling research. When you have real users doing real tasks, you learn where the model actually fails, and those failures are often much more interesting than anything you'd come up with on a benchmark. Someone's trying to get a model to work through a messy spreadsheet, or follow a long multi-step instruction, and it quietly drops a constraint halfway through. That's a research problem. Some of the best work I've seen started as a product complaint.

So practically, that means mixed teams, shared evals, and a lot of tolerance for ambiguity about who owns what. Researchers have to be okay with shipping something that isn't fully understood yet, and product folks have to be okay with the ground shifting under them every few months. The tension is real, but I'd rather manage that tension than have the two groups be politely separate.

r001.rationale: The response says research capabilities should flow into products, but it does not identify this as a goal shared by Google Brain and Andrew Dai’s current company.

astra-6.text:
I think of them as a feedback loop. Frontier research expands what’s possible, and product development helps us understand which capabilities are actually useful to people—and where they still fall short. When you put a model in people’s hands, you discover problems that aren’t always obvious from a benchmark, and those problems can inform the next round of research.

At the same time, you need room for research that doesn’t have an immediate product application. If everything is driven by the next launch, you can miss longer-term opportunities. The challenge is keeping those teams closely connected while giving them space to work on different time horizons.

r001.rationale: The response says putting a model in people’s hands helps reveal useful capabilities and problems, but it does not identify this as a goal shared by Google Brain and Andrew Dai’s current company.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as closely connected. Frontier research expands what’s possible, while product development helps us understand which capabilities are actually useful and where they still fall short. Getting something into people’s hands can reveal problems that aren’t obvious from a research benchmark.

At the same time, research needs room to explore ideas that don’t have an immediate product application. So the goal is a strong feedback loop: products inform the research questions, and research creates opportunities for products we couldn’t have built before.

r001.rationale: The response says product development helps put capabilities into people’s hands, but it does not identify Google Brain or state that this is a goal shared with Andrew Dai’s current company.
